title: Browser Security Notes: SOP, CSRF, SameSite and CORS
summary: Quick revision notes on how the same-origin policy, CSRF defences, SameSite cookies and CORS fit together, from the mental model to preflight and the misconfigurations that get exploited.

chapters.title: Same-Origin Policy Mental Model
points: Origin = scheme + host + port; https://a.com and http://a.com, a.com:8443 or b.a.com are all different origins
SOP blocks scripts on one origin from READING responses from another origin; it does not stop the request from being sent
Cross-origin embedding is allowed (img, script, link, form POST, iframe display), but reading the contents is not
SOP vs CORS: SOP is the browser default that restricts, CORS is the opt-in server mechanism that relaxes it for reads; neither protects the server from direct requests like curl
Interview Point: What exactly is an origin? Does SOP stop a cross-site request from being sent? Why does a cross-site form POST still work under SOP?

chapters.title: CSRF Attacks and CSRF Tokens
points: CSRF: the victim's browser automatically attaches cookies to a forged cross-site request, so the server sees an authenticated state-changing action; the attacker never reads the response
Needs three things: cookie-based auth, a state-changing endpoint, and predictable request parameters
Synchronizer token: server stores a random per-session token and requires it in a hidden field or header; the attacker cannot read it because of SOP
Double-submit cookie: token sent in both a cookie and a header or body, and the server compares them (sign or HMAC it to stop subdomain cookie injection)
Interview Point: Why does a CSRF token defeat CSRF? Why must GET never change state? Does a JSON API with cookie auth need CSRF protection?

chapters.title: SameSite Cookies and Defence in Depth
points: SameSite=Strict: cookie never sent on cross-site requests, including top-level link navigation from another site

SameSite=Lax: cookie sent on cross-site top-level GET navigations only, not on cross-site POST, iframe or fetch; this is the default only in Chromium-based browsers when the attribute is unset (Firefox and Safari do not apply it), so always set it explicitly
SameSite=None requires the Secure attribute and sends the cookie on all cross-site requests, which brings back CSRF exposure
Same-site is based on the registrable domain (eTLD+1), so subdomains count as same-site even though they are different origins; a compromised subdomain can still attack
Interview Point: Strict vs Lax: when would a user lose their login? Is SameSite a full replacement for CSRF tokens? Origin vs site?

chapters.title: CORS Headers and Preflight Requests
points: The browser sends an Origin header; the server replies with Access-Control-Allow-Origin naming that origin (or *) and the browser decides whether JS may read the response
Simple requests (GET, HEAD, POST with form or text content types and no custom headers) skip preflight; a custom header, PUT/DELETE or Content-Type: application/json triggers one

Preflight: the browser sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers; the server answers Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers and Access-Control-Max-Age to cache the result

Credentialed requests need fetch credentials:'include' and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, and the allowed origin must be explicit, never *; non-simple response headers need Access-Control-Expose-Headers
Interview Point: When is a preflight sent? Why can't * be used with credentials? Does CORS protect the server from CSRF?

chapters.title: Common CORS Misconfigurations
points: Reflecting the request Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Allow-Credentials: true lets any site read authenticated responses
Weak allowlist checks, such as endsWith('example.com') or a substring match, are bypassed by evil-example.com or example.com.evil.com
Trusting the null origin (sandboxed iframes and file:// pages can send it) gives attackers a way in
Missing Vary: Origin when the allowed origin is dynamic lets caches serve one origin's CORS headers to another
Interview Point: How would you exploit a reflected-origin CORS bug? Why is wildcard plus credentials rejected by browsers? How do you validate origins safely?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: SOP, CSRF, SameSite, CORS
points: Origin = scheme+host+port; site = scheme + eTLD+1 (ignores port and subdomain); SOP blocks reads, not sends
CSRF defences in order: SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies, anti-CSRF token on state-changing requests, check Origin/Referer, no state changes on GET
Cookie flags to remember: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax set explicitly (only Chromium defaults to Lax), None only with Secure
CORS headers: Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods, Allow-Headers, Allow-Credentials, Expose-Headers, Max-Age, plus Vary: Origin
Debug rule: a CORS error is the browser blocking the read, so check the response headers and the OPTIONS preflight status in DevTools; never reflect Origin, trust null, or pair * with credentials
